div.div:
Why two Azure regions - the hub/spoke split is forced, not a preference
The ExpressRoute gateway must sit in East US: a MultiCloud-tier circuit is evaluated as a Local circuit and attaches only to the region matching its peering location (useast). But this subscription has no VM capacity in East US - all 1420 sizes are restricted at type: Location, which is capacity and not quota - so the VM had to land in East US 2. Gateways are not VMs, so only the VM had to move; the spoke reaches AWS through the hub gateway via peering with allow_gateway_transit and use_remote_gateways. If your subscription can build VMs in East US, set azure_location = "eastus" and the two VNets collapse into one.
Prefixes exchanged over the interconnect
▶ Azure advertises 10.100.0.0/24 (hub) and 10.100.1.0/24 (spoke). The spoke prefix only appears when the peering sets use_remote_gateways.
◀ AWS advertises 10.200.0.0/16. Seen on the gateway as Origin EBgp, asPath 12076-64512, across 4 ECMP next hops 10.100.0.4 - 10.100.0.7.
Both directions must be true independently. One missing direction fails ping one way only, which looks exactly like a firewall problem.
Measurement plane (dashed teal) - observes the path, never carries it
Two vantage points probe the same target, the AWS EC2 private IP: ci-mcilab-probe beside the gateway in the East US hub, and vm-mcilab-azure in the East US 2 spoke. Both POST their samples to the collector on 10.100.1.4:8080 across the hub/spoke peering. The dashboard on that same port is reachable from the VM public IP, restricted by NSG to the operator /32.
The hub vantage point is roughly 4.1 ms faster at p50 - that difference is the latency cost of the forced region split. Nothing here touches the circuit, the interconnect, the DXGW or the gateway.
